lines.text: Wednesday, the sixth of April, nineteen sixty-six. A school oval in the south-east of Melbourne. Two physical education classes are outside, and the bell for morning recess is minutes away. Then somebody looks up.
Some call it the biggest mass sighting in Australian history. Hundreds of children. Teachers. A silver disc, they say, that came down in a paddock, and men in suits who told everyone to keep quiet.
But a school day is a wonderful thing to investigate. It has a timetable, a roll, a staff room, and a local paper that wrote things down. So tonight we run this case like a school day, bell by bell.
Roll call. First period on the oval. Recess in the paddock. The staff room. The press. Detention for the weather balloon. And a final lesson on memory. Then the case gets a report card.
Every claim will be marked: evidence, unverified, or failed. And one question stays on the board. What did hundreds of schoolchildren actually see over Westall? Take your seats.

Roll call. Westall High School, in Clayton South, about twenty-one kilometres from the centre of Melbourne. Flat country. Low brick classrooms, a big sports oval, and two huge electricity pylons at the edges of the grounds.
It was the Wednesday before Easter. The first term finished the next afternoon, and then came two weeks of holidays. Students and teachers alike had their minds somewhere else.

And the sky above that school was never empty. Moorabbin Airport lay about four kilometres away, one of the busiest little airports in the country. Every student knew what a light aircraft looked and sounded like.

To the south lay The Grange, a patch of scrub, paddocks and pine trees. Farmers grazed cattle there. The school ran its cross-country races through it. Remember this place. It matters in a few minutes.

This was also the age of the space race, the Cold War, and flying saucers in the headlines. Everyone in nineteen sixty-six knew exactly what a flying saucer was supposed to look like. Keep that in mind too.
That is the stage. Now, what happened on the oval? The bell goes. First period begins.
First period. At about a quarter past ten, by one careful account, two groups of Form One and Form Three students were out on the oval for sport, with their teachers, among them Miss Jeanette Muir.
Then came shouting. A few students saw it first. Silent, silver or grey, domed on top, like an upside-down bowl. About the size of one car, or two. And no sound at all.
Some say it passed low over the oval, as low as the gum trees and the goalposts. Others say it stayed far off, beyond the pines. Already, two different versions of the same morning.

A girl ran into a science lesson shouting that there were flying saucers outside. Her teacher, Andrew Greenwood, was not pleased. But when the recess bell rang, he took his class out to see for himself.

Greenwood gave a detailed account to the local paper. He saw a silvery streak, like a thin beam of light, about half the length of a light aircraft. It moved from side to side, and its size seemed to change.

And then the planes. Five light aircraft, he said, chasing it in a game of cat and mouse that lasted twenty minutes. On twenty-first of April the paper asked on its front page: who were the five pilots?
The Age asked around. No commercial, private or Air Force pilot had reported anything unusual that morning. If five aircraft had been chasing something, nobody has ever said it was them.
Later retellings add more. Some witnesses saw one object. Some saw two. Some, three. It rose, they say, and vanished in a blink, leaving the five planes behind as if standing still.

One account survives from that April, an anonymous report in a student magazine from a nearby primary school. It guessed the craft might be military aircraft from Moorabbin. It was reprinted that June in a saucer-society review.
And now the craft, they said, dropped down behind the pine trees. The recess bell had rung. Dozens of students jumped the fence and ran for The Grange.
Recess. Across a dirt road, over paddocks, toward the pines. Teachers shouted for them to come back. Many did not hear, or did not listen. It was the most exciting morning of their lives.
A few witnesses remember girls who fainted, and an ambulance on the school oval. Some remember a shape lifting off as they arrived. Others arrived just after, and saw only grass.
What they found, many say, was a circle. Flattened grass, swirled in one direction. Some called it burnt. Some said boiled. Some said three circles, not one. The details never agreed.
One student, interviewed by the local paper at the time, thought it looked like the wind had flattened it. In nineteen sixty-six, that was one of the very few records of the circle itself.
The woodwork teacher, Gerry Shepherd, had not seen a saucer. But he knew The Grange well. In twenty years he never saw a circle like that one, he later said, before or since.
Decades later, a firefighter and a civil defence officer told researchers their crews were sent to The Grange that day, to something reported coming down. No call log has been shown to the public.
Here is the first strange thing. Hundreds of children, in an age of cheap cameras. And yet no authenticated photograph or film of the object, or the circle, has ever been made public.

Three days later, on the ninth of April, Air Force personnel and saucer enthusiasts visited the field. They reported nothing of interest. The landowner then burned the paddock, to keep people off his property.
Some versions say the military burned the evidence. The farmer's own explanation was simpler. Either way, the one place that could have held a physical clue was gone.
So by the end of recess: lights or discs in the sky, a vague circle, and nothing anyone could pick up. But the school day was not over. Next, the staff room.

The staff room. The headmaster, Frank Samblebe, called the students together. According to many witnesses, he told them that flying saucers did not exist, and that they were not to talk about this morning.

Some recall strangers standing beside him. Dark suits, say some. Dark blue uniforms, say others. All agree, they were from the Government. Some students say they were questioned in the headmaster's office.
Notice what kind of evidence this is. Every word of it comes from memory, decades later. So we go back to what was printed in nineteen sixty-six.

The Dandenong Journal, fourteenth of April. Front page: Flying Saucer Mystery, School Silent. The school, it reported, would allow no further interviews, and had asked students and staff not to talk to reporters.

Three weeks later, the same paper printed the headmaster's own explanation. The flood of callers, he said, from the Air Force down to the Flying Saucer Association, was interrupting the children's studies.
Read that twice. A headmaster protecting his school, say the skeptics. A silencing, say the believers. And the very same newspaper line supports both stories. That is how this case behaves.

Later accounts go much further. Twenty-four witnesses have told researchers of police or soldiers at the school or the paddock, of cordons, of Geiger counters. None of this appears in the papers of that April.
And the official files? No Air Force, police or government file about Westall has been publicly found. Either nothing was written, or what was written is missing. Silence can mean both.
The press. Two newspapers matter. The first is the big Melbourne daily, The Age, and its short item on the seventh of April, with a very plain headline: Object, Perhaps Balloon.
The Weather Bureau, it said, had released a balloon from Laverton at half past eight that morning, and the westerly wind could have carried it into the area where the object was seen.
The second paper is the local Dandenong Journal, the only one to dig in. Brian Dunning, a skeptic, notes that in its first reports it named one teacher and several students, not hundreds.
A saucer society, the Victorian Flying Saucer Research Society, inspected the scene and interviewed witnesses that April. But no full account was published then. The thick files came much later.

Researcher Shane Ryan began collecting testimony in the two thousands. By the sixtieth anniversary, his count stood at one hundred and forty-two who saw the objects, one hundred and ninety-seven who saw marks on the ground, and seventy-seven who saw both.

His work fed a two thousand and ten documentary, Westall sixty-six. Remarkably, it was later used in Australian classrooms as a lesson in critical analysis: how do we judge a popular story about the past?
Detention. Time to put the ordinary explanations on trial. There are two main ones, and they are each stronger than most believers admit, and weaker than most skeptics claim. First, the balloon.

Between nineteen sixty and sixty-nine, Australia and the United States flew HIBAL balloons, large silver research balloons carrying instruments to sample the air for radiation after the British nuclear tests at Maralinga.

Researcher Keith Basterfield found papers pointing to a HIBAL flight planned from Mildura on the fifth of April, the day before Westall. But the report on that launch, and where it landed, has not been found.
The theory fits some details. A silver shape, a parachute, a metal payload, and, in this programme, a light aircraft following to track it. The trouble is, no document ties any HIBAL to Westall.

Critics add two more problems. A heavy payload at low level would hardly dart about faster than aircraft. And a recent review of the weather data, reported for the sixtieth anniversary, says the weather data does not stack up.

The second explanation came from a letter in the Dandenong Journal, signed only by a former Air Force navigator. Greenwood's chase, he wrote, matched a trainer towing a nylon target drogue while other pilots practised following it.

A target drogue would explain a silvery streak, a cat-and-mouse chase, and why pilots saw nothing odd in a routine exercise. But no record shows such an exercise took place that morning. It remains a possibility only.
And the alien version? It needs a craft that landed, left a circle, and left again. No craft, no sample, no radar, no photograph. Not one piece of hardware. Everything it relies on is memory.
So maybe the answer is not one thing. Dunning suggests a balloon for the first half of the sighting and aircraft for the second. Possible. But it is a guess built on two guesses.

Final lesson: memory. In nineteen sixty-six these witnesses were twelve to sixteen years old. The first systematic interviews came in the early two thousands. Four decades of retelling lay between the oval and the notebook.

Skeptic Richard Saunders, reviewing the case in twenty twenty-six, calls it memory fragility, false memory and memory contagion. Yet he also says he believes something happened. He just thinks the details grew in the telling.
The reports from the time do differ. A weather balloon. A humped silver disc. One object, or five. One circle, or many. Every group of honest witnesses ends up with a slightly different story.
And yet, listen to them at sixty years on. These are not people selling a story. Many have carried it quietly all their lives, and say only that they would like an answer from the government.
What survives every filter? A silent, silvery object, seen by many people from a school in broad daylight. Light aircraft in the area. The rest is thin, contradictory, or missing.

Calls for a fresh inquiry are growing, with researchers pointing to Department of Supply files they say are still unopened. If those papers exist, they could end this argument. Until then, it stays open.
Report card. Time to mark the Westall case.
Many people saw something odd that morning: evidence. Reported in print within days: evidence. Accounts that agree on details: only partly. A burned landing circle: unverified, no photo, no sample.
Military cordon and men in suits: nothing in the 1966 record. Balloon or drogue: plausible but unproven. Alien craft: no evidence at all.

The verdict. Incomplete. Something unusual really was seen over Westall, by real people, and the story was told at once. But nothing in the record shows a craft from elsewhere. Most likely a mix of balloon and aircraft. See me after class.
Today, The Grange has a children's playground shaped like a silver flying saucer, with red slides. A small joke from the people of Westall. And a reminder that this story is, above all, theirs.
Next case: a policeman on a lonely New Mexico road, an egg-shaped craft in a gully, and a burned bush. Was it real, or a hoax? We open that file next.
What do you think the children saw? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next ancient mystery put to the test.
